units.text: Adult female weevils of an unknown age were selected for observation. Female weevils were chosen because males spent the majority of their time in mate location behaviour, whereas the movements of females seemed primarily to be associated with feeding or sheltering. Each weevil was observed continuously for 9–10 h, except where it flew off during the observation and was lost. Observations began between 06.30 and 07.00 hours and ended between 16.00 and 17.00 hours (dawn was at 06.00 hours and dusk at 18.00 hours). Temperatures during the days of observation were between 25 and 29°C. The observations were recorded in 1995 using a notebook and a stopwatch, and in 1996 using a lap-top computer programmed as an event recorder. The behavioural elements recorded were categorized as: (1) quiescent; (2) walking; (3) feeding; (4) defaecating; or (5) flying. Data were recorded continuously to a temporal resolution of 1 s during the second year and 2–3 s during the first year. A record was kept of each leaf eaten or walked upon in succession by attaching a PVC tape label to one of the leaflets or the petiole. After the observations were completed, the weevil was captured and the various leaves collected. In 1996, the weevils were also taken back to the laboratory, weighed and measured and then released. In 1995, the weevils were frozen and freeze-dried, but not wet-weighed. Leaf samples were prepared for later allelochemical and nutrient analysis and subsequent correlation with elements of the feeding patterns, the results of which are to be presented elsewhere.

Eleven weevils were observed individually in 1995 and 15 in 1996. The behaviour of the weevils did not differ significantly between the two years, when the average meal durations (P = 0.899) and intermeal intervals (P = 0.249) were compared using a Mann–Whitney test. Therefore, data from the two years were pooled in the following analyses. Of the total number of weevils observed, a complete 10-h record was gained for 15 and the remaining 10 insects were observed for between 2 and 9 h.

To investigate whether there were changes in the structure of the feeding pattern throughout the day, Fisher-transformed, Pearson's correlation coefficients were calculated for each weevil, both for the duration of meals and also the duration of the preceding and following intermeal interval, against the time during the day when each meal began. Mean values of these correlation coefficients were derived across the population of weevils and tested against zero in a one sample, two-tailed t-test. Such a test avoids the problem of having too few data per insect in the majority of cases to generate individually significant correlations. Pooling data across insects is invalid because it confounds differences between individuals with relationships occurring between variables within insects (Simpson, 1990; Raubenheimer & Bernays, 1993). No time trend was evident for meal duration or intermeal interval (meal duration: mean Pearson's r=-0.22; SD=0.57; P=0.130; preprandial intermeal interval: mean Pearson's r=0.21; SD=0.67; P=0.160; postprandial intermeal interval: mean Pearson's r=0.21; SD 0.58; P=0.668).

The pattern of feeding also appeared not to be influenced by the size of weevil. Neither meal duration nor intermeal interval was correlated with weevil size (mean Pearson's $r = -0.07$; $P = 0.744$; and mean Pearson's $r = 0.19$; $P = 0.090$, for those weevils that were wet weighed vs. mean meal duration and intermeal interval, respectively; and mean Pearson's $r = 0.09$; $P = 0.775$; and mean Pearson's $r = -0.27$; $P = 0.450$ for those that were dry weighed).

The feeding patterns demonstrated by the weevils are the simplest in temporal structure and the most regular of any reported to date in an insect (or indeed anything else, so far as we are aware). The pattern of feeding was not affected by time of day during the observation period. Chapman & Beerling (1990) found that first-instar Schistocerca americana increased their intake from morning to evening, while Simpson (1982) found no time effect over the photophase for Locusta migratoria. The grasshopper T. eques fed only at specific times of the morning and early afternoon (Raubenheimer & Bernays, 1993).
